templates.pattern: The intensity of a sound wave is [I] × 10⁻¹² W/m². Calculate the sound level in decibels. (Threshold of hearing I₀ = 10⁻¹² W/m²)
templates.explanation:
Sound level = 10 × log₁₀(I ÷ I₀)
= 10 × log₁₀([I] × 10⁻¹² ÷ 10⁻¹²)
= 10 × log₁₀([I])
= [RESULT] dB

The decibel scale is logarithmic. An increase of 10 dB represents a tenfold increase in intensity. Normal conversation is about 60 dB.

templates.pattern: A standing wave is set up on a string of length [L] m. The wave is vibrating in its [N]th harmonic. Calculate the wavelength in metres.
templates.explanation:
For the nth harmonic on a string fixed at both ends:
λ = 2L ÷ n
= 2 × [L] ÷ [N]
= [2*L] ÷ [N]
= [RESULT] m

Higher harmonics have shorter wavelengths and higher frequencies. The nth harmonic has n antinodes along the string.

templates.pattern: A string of length [L] m vibrates in its [N]th harmonic with a wave speed of [V] m/s. Calculate the frequency of this harmonic in Hz.
templates.explanation:
Frequency of nth harmonic = n × v ÷ 2L
= [N] × [V] ÷ (2 × [L])
= [N] × [V] ÷ [2*L]
= [RESULT] Hz

The nth harmonic frequency is exactly n times the fundamental frequency. Harmonics give musical instruments their characteristic timbre.

templates.pattern: A pipe closed at one end has a length of [L] m and a wave speed of [V] m/s. Calculate the frequency of the fundamental mode in Hz.
templates.explanation:
For a pipe closed at one end:
Fundamental frequency f₁ = v ÷ 4L
= [V] ÷ (4 × [L])
= [V] ÷ [4*L]
= [RESULT] Hz

A closed pipe produces only odd harmonics. Its fundamental frequency is half that of an open pipe of the same length.

templates.pattern: A pipe open at both ends has a length of [L] m and a wave speed of [V] m/s. Calculate the frequency of the fundamental mode in Hz.
templates.explanation:
For a pipe open at both ends:
Fundamental frequency f₁ = v ÷ 2L
= [V] ÷ (2 × [L])
= [V] ÷ [2*L]
= [RESULT] Hz

An open pipe produces all harmonics. Both ends are antinodes. This gives open pipes a brighter, richer sound than closed pipes.

templates.pattern: A particle on a transverse wave has amplitude [A] m and frequency [F] Hz. Calculate the maximum speed of the particle in m/s.
templates.explanation:
Maximum particle speed = ωA = 2πfA
= 2 × π × [F] × [A]
= 2 × 3.14159 × [F] × [A]
= [RESULT] m/s

This is the maximum speed of a single particle oscillating about its rest position. It is not the same as wave speed.

templates.pattern: In a Young's double slit experiment the slit separation is [d] mm, the screen distance is [D] m and the wavelength of light is [LAM] nm. Calculate the fringe spacing in mm.
templates.explanation:
Fringe spacing W = λD ÷ d
= ([LAM] × 10⁻⁹ × [D]) ÷ ([d] × 10⁻³)
= [LAM] × [D] ÷ ([d] × 1000)
= [RESULT] mm

Smaller slit separation gives wider fringes. Longer wavelengths also give wider fringes.

templates.pattern: In a Young's double slit experiment the fringe spacing is [W] mm, the screen distance is [D] m and the slit separation is [d] mm. Calculate the wavelength of light used in nm.
templates.explanation:
Wavelength λ = W × d ÷ D
= ([W] × 10⁻³ × [d] × 10⁻³) ÷ [D]
= [W] × [d] × 1000 ÷ [D] nm
= [RESULT] nm

This is how the wavelength of light can be accurately measured using a double slit experiment.

templates.pattern: A wave has frequency [F] Hz and travels into a new medium where its wavelength becomes [L2] m. Calculate the speed of the wave in the new medium in m/s.
templates.explanation:
Wave speed in new medium = frequency × new wavelength
= f × λ₂
= [F] × [L2]
= [RESULT] m/s

Frequency stays constant when a wave crosses a boundary. The new speed is determined by the properties of the new medium.

templates.pattern: A stationary observer hears a frequency of [FO] Hz from an approaching source. The speed of sound is [V] m/s and the source speed is [VS] m/s. Calculate the true frequency emitted by the source in Hz.
templates.explanation:
Rearranging the Doppler formula f' = fv/(v-vs):
True frequency f = f' × (v − vs) ÷ v
= [FO] × ([V] − [VS]) ÷ [V]
= [FO] × [V-VS] ÷ [V]
= [RESULT] Hz

The observer hears a higher frequency than the true emitted frequency when the source is approaching.
